There was a fellow I knew once in Barcelona, odd fellow, used to call it his post-prandial. Well: cheers! Around the slabbed tables the tangle of wine-soaked breaths and rumbling stomachs. His breath hangs over our sauce-stained plates, the green fairy's fang of absinthe thrusting between his lips. Of Ireland, the warriors of Brian Boru, of hopes, conspiracies, of Arthur Griffith the nationalist, the mystical poet A.E., good shepherd of men. Trying to yoke me as his fellow revolutionary, our crimes our common cause. You're your father's son. I know the voice. His worn shirt, decorated with red flowers, trembles its Spanish tassels at his secrets. Drumont, famous French journalist — know what he called Queen Victoria? Old hag with the yellow teeth. Old ogress with the yellow teeth. Maud Gonne, beautiful woman, for the Fatherland. Millevoye, Félix Faure — know how Faure died? Lustful men. The Scandinavian girl, maid of all work, who rubs men naked in the bath at Uppsala. It's my job, she said, all the gentlemen. Not this gentleman, I said. Most indecent custom. A bath is a most private thing. I wouldn't let my brother, not even my own brother, it's most indecent. Green eyes, I see you. Fangs, I feel. Lustful people.

The blue fuse of his cigarette burns deadly between hands and burns clear. Loose tobacco shreds catch fire: a flame and acrid smoke light our corner. Raw cheekbones under his rebel's cap. How the rebel leader escaped, the real story. Disguised as a young bride, man in veil and orange blossoms, drove out the road to Malahide. He did, truly. Tales of lost leaders, the betrayed, wild escapes. Disguises snatched at, gone, not here.

Spurned lover. I was a strapping young lad at that time, I tell you. I'll show you my picture one day. I was, truly. A lover — for her love, for Ireland's love, he prowled with Colonel Richard Burke, chieftain of his clan, under the walls of Clerkenwell Prison and, crouching, saw a flame of vengeance hurl them upward in the fog. Shattered glass and toppling masonry. In gay Paris he hides, Egan of Paris, sought by no one save by me. Making his daily rounds: the dingy print shop, his three taverns, the Montmartre den where he sleeps short nights, in the street of the Golden Drop, decorated with flyblown photographs of the dead. Loveless, landless, wifeless. She is quite comfortably settled without her outcast man, the madam on the Street of the Lying Heart, with a canary and two male lodgers. Peachy cheeks, a striped skirt, frisky as a young thing. Spurned and undespairing. Tell Pat you saw me, won't you? I wanted to get poor Pat a job one time. My son, soldier of France. I taught him to sing The Boys of Kilkenny Are Stout Roaring Blades. Know that old tune? I taught Patrice that. Old Kilkenny: Saint Canice's city, Strongbow's castle on the River Nore. Goes like this. Oh, oh. He takes my hand, like Napper Tandy in the song.

Oh, oh the boys of
Kilkenny...
Weak wasting hand on mine. They have forgotten Kevin Egan, not he them. Remembering thee, O Zion.

He had come nearer the edge of the sea and wet sand slapped his boots. The new air greeted him, harping on wild nerves, wind of wild air carrying seeds of brightness. Wait — I'm not walking out to the Kish lighthouse, am I? He stopped suddenly, his feet beginning to sink slowly in the quaking soil. Turn back.

Turning, he scanned the shore southward, his feet sinking again slowly in new depressions. The cold domed room of the tower waits. Through the narrow windows the shafts of light move ever onward, slowly ever as my feet are sinking, creeping duskward across the floor. Blue dusk, nightfall, deep blue night. In the darkness of the dome they wait, their pushed-back chairs, my battered suitcase, around a table of abandoned plates. Who will clear them? He has the key. I will not sleep there when night comes. A shut door of a silent tower, entombing their blind bodies, the panther-dreaming Englishman and his gun dog. Call: no answer. He lifted his feet from the sucking sand and turned back by the wall of boulders. Take everything, keep everything. My soul walks with me, the form of forms. So in the moon's midnight watches I pace the path above the rocks, in dark silver, hearing Elsinore's tempting flood.

The flood is following me. I can watch it flow past from here. Better get back by the Poolbeg road to the strand. He climbed over the sedge and eel-like seaweed and sat on a stool of rock, resting his walking stick in a crevice.

A bloated carcass of a dog lay sprawled on bladder-wrack seaweed. Before him the side of a boat, sunk in sand. A coach stuck in sand — that's what the French critic Louis Veuillot called Théophile Gautier's prose. These heavy sands are language, tide and wind have silted here. And these, the stone heaps of dead builders, a warren of rat warrens. Hide gold there. Try it. You have some. Sands and stones. Weight of the past. Some giant's toys. Mind you don't get one good smack on the ear. I'm the bloody great giant who rolls all these bloody great boulders, bones for my stepping stones. Fee-fi-fo-fum. I smell the blood of an Irishman.

A point, a live dog, grew into sight running across the sweep of sand. Lord, is he going to attack me? Respect his freedom. You will not be master of others or their slave. I have my stick. Sit tight. From farther away, walking shoreward from the crested tide, figures, two. The two Marys — like those at Christ's tomb. They have tucked it safe among the bulrushes. Peekaboo. I see you. No, the dog. He is running back to them. Who?

Galleys of the Vikings ran here to beach, in quest of prey, their blood-beaked prows riding low on a molten pewter surf. Danish Vikings, gold neck-rings and hatchets aglitter on their chests, when the Irish king Malachi wore the collar of gold. A school of whales stranded in hot noon, spouting, floundering in the shallows. Then from the starving walled city a horde of ragged dwarfs, my people, with butchers' knives, running, climbing, hacking in green blubbery whale meat. Famine, plague and slaughters. Their blood is in me, their passions my waves. I moved among them on the frozen River Liffey, I, a changeling, among the sputtering bonfires. I spoke to no one: none to me.

The dog's bark ran toward him, stopped, ran back. Dog of my enemy. I just stood there pale, silent, surrounded by barking. Meditating terrible things. A man in a primrose-colored jacket, fortune's favorite, smiled at my fear. Is that what you pine for — the bark of their applause? Pretenders: living their lives. The Bruce's brother, Thomas Fitzgerald the silken knight, Perkin Warbeck, York's false heir in breeches of white-rose ivory, wonder of a day, and Lambert Simnel with a train of nuns and camp followers, a kitchen boy crowned king. All kings' sons. Paradise of pretenders then and now. He saved men from drowning and you tremble at a dog's yelping. But the courtiers who mocked the poet Guido in his own city's church were on their own turf. House of... We don't want any of your medieval obscurities. Would you do what he did? A boat would be near, a life buoy. Naturally — put there for you. Would you or wouldn't you? The man who drowned nine days ago off Maiden's Rock. They are waiting for him now. The truth, spit it out. I would want to. I would try. I am not a strong swimmer. Water cold soft. When I put my face into it in the basin at Clongowes school. Can't see! Who's behind me? Out quickly, quickly! Do you see the tide flowing quickly in on all sides, sheeting the low sandbars quickly, shell-cocoa-colored? If I had solid ground under my feet. I want his life still to be his, mine to be mine. A drowning man. His human eyes scream to me out of the horror of his death. I... Together with him, down... I could not save her. Waters: bitter death: lost.
A woman and a man. I see her skirts. Pinned up, I bet.

Their dog ambled about a bank of thinning sand, trotting, sniffing on all sides. Looking for something lost in a past life. Suddenly he bolted like a hare, ears flung back, chasing the shadow of a low-skimming gull. The man's shrieked whistle struck his limp ears. He turned, bounded back, came nearer, trotted on twinkling legs. Like a heraldic deer on a tawny field, bounding, noble, free. At the lace-edge of the tide he halted with stiff forelegs, ears pointed seaward. His snout lifted, barking at the wave noise, herds of sea horses. They serpented toward his feet, curling, unfurling many crests, every ninth one breaking, splashing, from far, from farther out, waves and waves.

Cockle pickers. They waded a little way into the water and, stooping, dunked their bags and, lifting them again, waded out. The dog yelped, running to them, reared up and pawed them, dropping on all fours, rearing up again at them with mute bearish affection. Unheeded, he kept by them as they came toward drier sand, a rag of wolf's tongue red-panting from his jaws. His speckled body ambled ahead of them and then loped off at a calf's gallop. The carcass lay on his path. He stopped, sniffed, stalked round it, brother, nosing closer, went round it, sniffing rapidly like a dog all over the dead dog's bedraggled coat. Dog skull, dog sniff, eyes on the ground, moves toward one great goal. Ah, poor dogsbody! Here lies poor dogsbody's body.
—Tatters! Get away from that, you mongrel!

The cry brought him skulking back to his master and a blunt bootless kick sent him unharmed across a spit of sand, crouched in flight. He slunk back in a curve. He doesn't see me. Along the edge of the stone wall he lolloped, dawdled, smelled a rock and from under a cocked hind leg pissed against it. He trotted forward and, lifting his hind leg again, pissed quick and short at a rock he hadn't sniffed. The simple pleasures of the poor. His back paws then scattered the sand: then his front paws dabbled and delved. Something he buried there, his grandmother. He rooted in the sand, dabbling, delving, and stopped to listen to the air, scraped up the sand again with a fury of his claws, soon ceasing, a leopard, a panther, born of an illicit union, preying on the dead.

After he woke me last night — the same dream or was it? Wait. Open hallway. Street of prostitutes. Remember. Haroun al Rashid from the Arabian Nights. I'm almost getting it. That man led me, spoke. I was not afraid. The melon he held against my face. Smiled: sweet cream-fruit smell. That was the rule, he said. In. Come. Red carpet spread. You will see who.

Shouldering their bags they trudged, the dark-skinned wanderers. His blue-cold feet out of turned-up trousers slapped the clammy sand, a dull brick scarf strangling his unshaven neck. With a woman's steps she followed: the rogue and his wandering woman. Her pickings slung at her back. Loose sand and crushed shells caked on her bare feet. About her wind-raw face hair trailed. Behind her lord, his helpmate, tramping off to nowhere. When night hides her body's flaws she calls from an archway where dogs have fouled. Her fancy man is buying drinks for two Royal Dublin Fusiliers in O'Loughlin's pub in Blackpitts. Kiss her, trade slang with her in rogues' street talk, for oh, my sweet wanton darling! A she-devil's whiteness under her rank rags. Fumbally's lane that night: the smell of the tannery.

White your hands, red your mouth
And your body's soft and fine.
Let me lie with you then.
In the darkness hold and kiss.

Gloomy pleasure, as the pot-bellied monk Aquinas calls it, you old porcupine friar. Adam before the Fall made love and did not merely rut. Call away, let him say: your body's soft and fine. Language no worse than his own. Monks' words, rosary beads jangling at their belts: rogues' words, hard coins rattling in their pockets.
Passing now.

A sideways glance at my Hamlet hat. If I were suddenly naked here as I sit? I am not. Across the sands of all the world, followed by the sun's flaming sword, to the west, trekking to evening lands. She trudges, hauls, drags, pulls her load. A tide westering, moon-drawn, in her wake. Tides, with their myriad islands, within her, blood not mine, upon the wine-dark sea. Behold the handmaid of the moon. In sleep the wet sign calls her hour, bids her rise. Bridal bed, childbed, bed of death, ghost-candled. All flesh shall come to you. He comes, pale vampire, through storm his eyes, his bat sails bloodying the sea, mouth to her mouth's kiss.
Here. Put a pin in that thought, will you? My notebook. Mouth to her kiss. No. Must be two of them. Stick them together. Mouth to her mouth's kiss.

His lips shaped and mouthed fleshless lips of air: mouth to her womb. Womb, all-wombing tomb. His mouth molded outgoing breath, unspoken: ooeeehah: roar of planets plunging catastrophically, globed, blazing, roaring wayawayawayawayaway. Paper. The banknotes, damn them. Old Deasy's letter. Here. Thanking you for the hospitality — tear the blank end off. Turning his back to the sun he bent far over a table of rock and scribbled words. That's twice I forgot to take blank slips from the library counter.

His shadow lay over the rocks as he bent, ending. Why not endless to the farthest star? Darkly they are there behind this light, darkness shining in the brightness, the constellation Cassiopeia, other worlds. Here I sit with my diviner's rod of ash wood, in borrowed sandals, by day beside a dull sea, unseen, in violet night walking beneath a sky of strange stars. I throw this finished shadow from me, the inescapable human shape, call it back. Endless, would it be mine, form of my form? Who watches me here? Who anywhere will ever read these written words? Signs on a white field. Somewhere to someone in your most lyrical voice. The philosopher Bishop Berkeley took the veil of appearances out of his top hat: the veil of space with colored patterns woven on it. Hold on. Colors on a flat surface: yes, that's right. Flat I see, then think distance, near, far, flat I see, east, back. Ah, see now! It falls back suddenly, frozen in three dimensions. Click does the trick. You find my words dark. Darkness is in our souls, don't you think? More lyrically. Our souls, shame-wounded by our sins, cling to us yet more, as a woman to her lover clinging, the more the more.

She trusts me, her hand gentle, the long-lashed eyes. Now where the blue hell am I leading her beyond the veil of appearances? Into the inescapable reality of the inescapable visible. She, she, she. What she? The young woman at the bookshop window on Monday looking in for one of the alphabet-titled books you were going to write. The keen glance you gave her. Her wrist through the braided loop of her parasol handle. She lives in Leeson Park with a companion and dainty dishes, a literary lady. Tell that to someone else, Stevie: pick me up at a party. Bet she wears those God-awful corsets and yellow stockings, darned with lumpy wool. Talk about dumpy women — forget about it. Where are your wits?
Touch me. Soft eyes. Soft soft soft hand. I am lonely here. Oh, touch me soon, now. What is that word known to all men? I am quiet here alone. Sad too. Touch, touch me.

He lay back at full stretch over the sharp rocks, cramming the scribbled note and pencil into a pocket, his hat tilted down over his eyes. That is Kevin Egan's gesture I just made, nodding for his nap, his sabbath sleep. And God saw. And it was very good. Hey! Good morning. Welcome as the flowers in May. Under its leaf he watched through peacock-twittering lashes the southward-moving sun. I am caught in this burning scene. Pan's hour, the faun's noon. Among gum-heavy serpent-plants, milk-oozing fruits, where on the tawny waters leaves lie wide. Pain is far.
And no more turn aside and brood.

His gaze brooded on his broad-toed boots, a rich man's cast-offs, side by side. He counted the creases of rucked leather where another's foot had nested warm. The foot that beat the ground in dance, the foot I dislike. But you were delighted when Esther Osvalt's shoe fit you: girl I knew in Paris. Oh, what a pretty little foot! A true friend, a soul brother: Wilde's love that dare not speak its name. His arm: Cranly's arm. He will leave me now. And the blame? I am as I am. All or not at all.

In long loops from the Cock lake the water flowed full, covering in green-gold the lagoons of sand, rising, flowing. My walking stick will float away. I shall wait. No, they will pass on, passing, rubbing against the low rocks, swirling, passing. Better get this business over quickly. Listen: a four-worded wave-speech: seesoo, hrss, rsseeiss, ooos. Powerful breath of waters amid sea-snakes, rearing horses, rocks. In cups of rocks it slops: flop, slop, slap: bounded in barrels. And spent, its speech ceases. It flows purling, widely flowing, floating foam-pool, flower unfurling.

Under the up-swelling tide he saw the writhing weeds lift languidly and sway reluctant arms, lifting their petticoats in whispering water, swaying and upturning shy silver fronds. Day by day: night by night: lifted, flooded and let fall. Lord, they are weary; and, whispered to, they sigh. Saint Ambrose heard it, the sigh of leaves and waves, waiting, awaiting the fullness of their times, suffering injuries day and night and groaning. Gathered to no end; vainly then released, flowing forth, winding back: drawn by the moon. Weary too in the sight of lovers, lustful men; a naked woman gleaming in her chambers, she draws a net of waters.

Five fathoms out there. Full fathom five thy father lies. At one o'clock, they said. Found drowned. High water at Dublin bar. Driving before it a loose drift of rubble, drifting schools of fish, silly shells. A corpse rising salt-white from the undertow, bobbing a pace a pace a porpoise landward. There he is. Hook it quick. Pull. Sunk though he be beneath the watery floor. We have him. Easy now.

Bag of corpse-gas sopping in foul brine. A quiver of minnows, fat of a spongy morsel, flash through the slits of his buttoned trouser fly. God becomes man becomes fish becomes barnacle goose becomes featherbed mountain. Dead men's breaths I, living, breathe; I tread dead dust, devour foul remains from all the dead. Hauled stiff over the side of a boat he breathes upward the stench of his green grave, his rotting nostrils snoring to the sun.

A sea-change this, brown eyes turned salt-blue. Sea-death, mildest of all deaths known to man. Old Father Ocean. Prize of Paris: beware of imitations. Just give it a fair trial. We enjoyed ourselves immensely.

Come. I'm thirsty. Clouding over. No black clouds anywhere though, are there? Thunderstorm. All-bright he falls, proud lightning of the intellect, Lucifer, I say, who knows no setting. No. My pilgrim's hat and staff and my sandal shoes. Where? To evening lands. Evening will find itself.

He took the handle of his walking stick, lunging with it softly, dallying still. Yes, evening will find itself in me, without me. All days make their end. By the way, next — when is it? Tuesday will be the longest day. Of all the glad new year, mother, the rum tum tiddledy tum. Tennyson, gentleman poet. Indeed. For the old hag with the yellow teeth — that's what they called Queen Victoria. And Monsieur Drumont, gentleman journalist. Indeed. My teeth are very bad. Why, I wonder. Feel. That one is going too. Shells — teeth like shells. Ought I go to a dentist, I wonder, with that money? That one. This one. Toothless Kinch, the superman. Why is that, I wonder, or does it mean something perhaps?
My handkerchief. He threw it. I remember. Did I not pick it up?
His hand groped vainly in his pockets. No, I didn't. Better buy one.
He placed the dry snot picked from his nostril on a ledge of rock, carefully. As for the rest, let whoever wants to look.
Behind me. Perhaps there is someone.

He turned his face over his shoulder, looking back. Moving through the air, the tall masts of a three-masted ship, her sails furled up on the yards, homeward bound, upstream, silently moving, a silent ship.
— II —

chapters.title: Episode 4 — Calypso
paragraphs: Mr Leopold Bloom ate with relish the inner organs of beasts and fowls. He liked thick giblet soup, nutty gizzards, a stuffed roast heart, liver slices fried with breadcrumbs, fried cod roe. Most of all he liked grilled mutton kidneys which gave to his palate a fine tang of faintly scented urine.

Kidneys were on his mind as he moved about the kitchen softly, setting up his wife's breakfast things on the bumpy tray. Cold light and air filled the kitchen but out of doors gentle summer morning everywhere. Made him feel a bit peckish.
The coals were reddening.

Another slice of bread and butter: three, four: right. She didn't like her plate full. Right. He turned from the tray, lifted the kettle off the hob and set it sideways on the fire. It sat there, dull and squat, its spout sticking out. Cup of tea soon. Good. Mouth dry. The cat walked stiffly around a leg of the table with tail held high.
—Meow!
—Oh, there you are, Mr Bloom said, turning from the fire.
The cat meowed in answer and stalked again stiffly around a leg of the table, meowing. Just how she stalks across my writing table. Purr. Scratch my head. Purr.

Mr Bloom watched curiously, kindly, the lithe black form. Clean to see: the gloss of her sleek hide, the white button under the base of her tail, the green flashing eyes. He bent down to her, his hands on his knees.
—Milk for the pussycat, he said.
—Meow! the cat cried.

They call them stupid. They understand what we say better than we understand them. She understands everything she wants to. Vindictive too. Cruel. Her nature. Curious how mice never squeal. They seem to like it. Wonder what I look like to her. Height of a tower? No, she can jump me.
—Afraid of the chickens she is, he said teasingly. Afraid of the cluck-clucks. I never saw such a stupid pussycat as the pussycat.
—Meow! the cat said loudly.

She blinked up out of her greedy, half-closing eyes, meowing plaintively and long, showing him her milk-white teeth. He watched the dark eye-slits narrowing with greed until her eyes were green stones. Then he went to the dresser, took the jug the milkman had just filled for him, poured warm bubbly milk on a saucer and set it slowly on the floor.
—Gurrhr! she cried, running to lap.

He watched the whiskers shining wiry in the weak light as she dipped three times and licked lightly. Wonder if it's true that if you clip their whiskers they can't catch mice afterward. Why? They shine in the dark, perhaps, the tips. Or kind of feelers in the dark, perhaps.

He listened to her lapping. Ham and eggs, no. No good eggs during this drought. Need pure fresh water. Thursday: not a good day either for a mutton kidney at Buckley's. Fried with butter, a shake of pepper. Better a pork kidney at Dlugacz's butcher shop. While the kettle is boiling. She lapped slower, then licked the saucer clean. Why are their tongues so rough? To lap better, all porous holes. Nothing she can eat? He glanced around. No.

On quietly creaking boots he went up the staircase to the hall, paused by the bedroom door. She might like something tasty. Thin bread and butter she likes in the morning. Still perhaps: once in a while.
He said softly in the bare hall:
—I'm going round the corner. Be back in a minute.
And when he had heard his voice say it he added:
—You don't want anything for breakfast?
A sleepy soft grunt answered:
—Mm.

No. She didn't want anything. He heard then a warm heavy sigh, softer, as she turned over and the loose brass rings of the bedstead jingled. Must get those fixed, really. Pity. That bed came all the way from Gibraltar. She's forgotten whatever little Spanish she knew. Wonder what her father gave for it. Old style. Ah yes, of course. Bought it at the governor's auction. Got it cheap. Hard as nails at a bargain, old Major Tweedy. Yes, sir. At the siege of Plevna that was. I rose from the ranks, sir, and I'm proud of it. Still, he had brains enough to make a fortune in stamps. Now that was farsighted.

His hand took his hat from the peg over his initialed heavy overcoat and his secondhand waterproof from the lost property office. Stamps: little sticky pictures. Probably lots of officers are in on it too. Of course they are. The faded label in the crown of his hat told him silently: Plasto's high grade ha — the t worn off. He peeked quickly inside the leather headband. White slip of paper. Quite safe.

On the doorstep he felt in his hip pocket for the latchkey. Not there. In the trousers I took off last night. Must get it. I have my lucky potato though. Creaky wardrobe. No use disturbing her. She turned over sleepily that time. He pulled the front door to after him very quietly, more, till the flap at the bottom dropped gently over the threshold, a limp lid. Looks shut. All right till I come back anyhow.

He crossed to the sunny side, avoiding the loose cellar flap of number seventy-five. The sun was nearing the steeple of George's church. Going to be a warm day, I think. Especially in these black clothes, you feel it more. Black conducts — reflects — refracts, is it? — the heat. But I couldn't go in that light suit. Would look like a picnic outing. His eyelids sank quietly, often, as he walked in happy warmth. Boland's bread van delivering with trays our daily bread, but she prefers yesterday's turnovers, crisp crusty ones, hot. Makes you feel young. Somewhere in the east: early morning: setting off at dawn. Travel round in front of the sun, steal a day's march on him. Keep it up forever, never grow a day older technically. Walk along a strand, strange land, come to a city gate, sentry there, old soldier too, like old Tweedy's big moustaches, leaning on a long kind of spear. Wander through awninged streets. Turbaned faces going by. Dark caves of carpet shops, a big man, Turko the Terrible, seated cross-legged, smoking a coiled pipe. Cries of sellers in the streets. Drink water scented with fennel, sherbet. Stroll along all day. Might meet a robber or two. Well, deal with him. Getting on toward sundown. The shadows of the mosques among the pillars: a priest with a scroll rolled up. A shiver of the trees, a signal, the evening wind. I pass on. Fading gold sky. A mother watches me from her doorway. She calls her children home in their dark language. High wall: beyond it strings plucked. Night sky, moon, violet, color of Molly's new garters. Strings. Listen. A girl playing one of those instruments, what do you call them: dulcimers. I pass.

Probably not a bit like that really. The kind of stuff you read: in the track of the sun. Sunburst on the title page. He smiled, pleasing himself. What Arthur Griffith said about the headpiece over the Freeman's Journal editorial: a home-rule sun rising up in the northwest from the laneway behind the Bank of Ireland. He prolonged his pleased smile. Jewish touch that: home-rule sun rising up in the northwest.

He approached Larry O'Rourke's pub. From the cellar grating floated up the heavy gush of stout. Through the open doorway the bar leaked out whiffs of ginger, tea dust, biscuit crumbs. Good business, though: right at the end of the city traffic. For instance, M'Auley's down there: no good as a location. Of course, if they ran a tram line along the North Circular from the cattle market to the quays, property values would shoot up.

Bald head over the window blind. Shrewd old fellow. No use canvassing him for an ad. Still, he knows his own business best. There he is, sure enough, my bold Larry, leaning against the sugar bin in his shirtsleeves watching the barman mop up with bucket and rag. Simon Dedalus does a perfect imitation of him with his eyes screwed up. Do you know what I'm going to tell you? What's that, Mr O'Rourke? Do you know what? The Russians — they'd only be breakfast for the Japanese.
Stop and say a word: about the funeral perhaps. Sad thing about poor Dignam, Mr O'Rourke.
Turning into Dorset Street he said freshly in greeting through the doorway:
—Good day, Mr O'Rourke.
—Good day to you.
—Lovely weather, sir.
—It is indeed.

Where do these publicans get the money? Fresh-faced young barmen coming up from County Leitrim, rinsing empties and dealing with the old man in the cellar. Then, lo and behold, they blossom into successful businessmen. Then think of the competition. The general thirst. Good puzzle: try crossing Dublin without passing a pub. Can't save, they just can't. Getting tips off the drunks perhaps. Counting pennies here and there, dribs and drabs. Or making side deals on the wholesale orders perhaps. Doing a double shuffle with the sales reps. You square it with the boss and we'll split the deal, see?

How much would that work out to, off the porter in the month? Say ten barrels of stuff. Say he got ten percent off. Oh, more. Fifteen. He passed Saint Joseph's National School. Kids' clamor. Windows open. Fresh air helps memory. Or a song. A-B-C-D-E-F-G-K-L-M-O-P-Q-R-S-T-U-V-W. Boys, are they? Yes. Inishturk. Inishark. Inishboffin. At their geography. Mine. Slieve Bloom — my name on the map.

He halted before Dlugacz's window, staring at the strings of sausages, polonies, black and white puddings. Fifteen multiplied by. The figures whitened in his mind, unsolved: displeased, he let them fade. The shiny links, packed with forcemeat, fed his gaze and he breathed in tranquilly the lukewarm breath of cooked spicy pig's blood.

A kidney oozed blood drops on the willow-pattern dish: the last one. He stood beside the next-door girl at the counter. Would she buy it too, reading the items from a slip in her hand? Chapped hands: washing soda. And a pound and a half of Denny's sausages. His eyes rested on her vigorous hips. Woods, her name is. Wonder what he does for a living. Wife is getting on in years. New blood. No male visitors allowed. Strong pair of arms. Whacking a carpet on the clothesline. She does whack it, by George. The way her crooked skirt swings at each whack.
The sharp-eyed pork butcher folded the sausages he had snipped off with blotchy fingers, sausage-pink. Good solid meat there: like a corn-fed heifer.

He picked up a page from the pile of cut sheets: an ad for a model farm at Kinnereth on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Could become an ideal winter health resort. Moses Montefiore. I thought he was. Farmhouse, wall around it, blurred cattle grazing. He held the page away from him: interesting: read it closer, the title, the blurred grazing cattle, the page rustling. A young white heifer. Those mornings at the cattle market, the beasts lowing in their pens, branded sheep, the plop and fall of dung, the breeders in hobnailed boots trudging through the muck, slapping a palm on a ripe-meated hindquarter — there's a prime one — unpeeled switches in their hands. He held the page tilted patiently, bending his senses and his will, his soft distracted gaze at rest. The crooked skirt swinging, whack by whack by whack.
The pork butcher snapped two sheets from the pile, wrapped up her best sausages, and made a red grimace.
—Now, my miss, he said.
She held out a coin, smiling boldly, her thick wrist extended.
—Thank you, my miss. And one shilling and threepence change. For you, please?

Mr Bloom pointed quickly. To catch up and walk behind her if she went slowly, behind her swaying hips. Pleasant to see first thing in the morning. Hurry up, damn it. Make hay while the sun shines. She stood outside the shop in sunlight and sauntered lazily to the right. He sighed down his nose: they never understand. Soda-chapped hands. Crusty toenails too. Brown religious scapulars in tatters, protecting her both ways. The sting of being ignored glowed to weak pleasure within his breast. For another man: a constable off duty cuddling her in Eccles Lane. They like them big. Prime sausage. Oh please, Mr Policeman, I'm lost in the woods.
—Threepence, please.

His hand accepted the moist tender organ and slid it into a side pocket. Then it fetched up three coins from his trouser pocket and laid them on the rubber mat. They lay, were read quickly and quickly slid, coin by coin, into the till.
—Thank you, sir. Another time.
A spark of eager fire from the butcher's foxy eyes thanked him. He withdrew his gaze after a moment. No: better not: another time.
—Good morning, he said, moving away.
—Good morning, sir.
No sign of the girl. Gone. What matter?

He walked back along Dorset Street, reading gravely. Agendath Netaim: planters' company. To purchase waste sandy tracts from the Turkish government and plant with eucalyptus trees. Excellent for shade, fuel, and construction. Orange groves and immense melon fields north of Jaffa. You pay eighty marks and they plant an acre of land for you with olives, oranges, almonds, or citrons. Olives cheaper: oranges need artificial irrigation. Every year you get a share of the crop. Your name entered for life as owner in the company register. Can pay ten down and the balance in yearly installments. Bleibtreustrasse 34, Berlin, W. 15.
Nothing doing. Still, there's an idea behind it.

He looked at the cattle, blurred in silver heat. Silver-powdered olive trees. Quiet long days: pruning, ripening. Olives packed in jars, eh? I have a few left from Andrews. Molly spitting them out. She knows the taste of them now. Oranges in tissue paper packed in crates. Citrons too. Wonder if poor Citron still lives on Saint Kevin's Parade. And Mastiansky with the old zither. Pleasant evenings we had then. Molly in Citron's basket chair. Nice to hold, cool waxy fruit, hold in the hand, lift it to the nostrils and smell the perfume. Like that, heavy, sweet, wild perfume. Always the same, year after year. They fetched high prices too, Moisel told me. Arbutus Place: Pleasants Street: pleasant old times. Must be without a flaw, he said. Coming all that way: Spain, Gibraltar, Mediterranean, the Levant. Crates lined up on the quayside at Jaffa, a clerk ticking them off in a book, dockworkers handling them barefoot in soiled overalls. There's what's-his-name, from. How do you do? Doesn't see me. Chap you know just well enough to nod to, bit of a bore. His back looks like that Norwegian captain's. Wonder if I'll run into him today. Watering cart. Trying to make it rain. On earth as it is in heaven.
A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, wholly. Grey. Far.

No, not like that. A barren land, bare waste. A volcanic lake, the Dead Sea: no fish, no weeds, sunk deep in the earth. No wind could lift those waves, grey metal, poisonous foggy waters. Brimstone they called it raining down: the cities of the plain: Sodom, Gomorrah, Edom. All dead names. A dead sea in a dead land, grey and old. Old now. It bore the oldest, the first race. A bent old woman crossed from Cassidy's pub, clutching a small bottle by the neck. The oldest people. Wandered far away over all the earth, captivity to captivity, multiplying, dying, being born everywhere. It lay there now. Now it could bear no more. Dead: an old woman's: the grey sunken womb of the world.
Desolation.

Grey horror seared his flesh. Folding the page into his pocket he turned into Eccles Street, hurrying homeward. Cold oils slid along his veins, chilling his blood: age crusting him with a salt cloak. Well, I am here now. Yes, I am here now. Morning mouth, bad images. Got up on the wrong side of the bed. Must begin again those Sandow exercises. Stand on my hands. Blotchy brown brick houses. Number eighty still empty. Why is that? Assessed value only twenty-eight pounds. Towers, Battersby, North, MacArthur: parlor windows plastered with for-sale signs. Bandages on a sore eye. To smell the gentle smoke of tea, the sizzle of the pan, sizzling butter. Be near her ample bed-warmed flesh. Yes, yes.
Quick warm sunlight came running from Berkeley Road, swiftly, in slim sandals, along the brightening footpath. Runs, she runs to meet me, a girl with gold hair on the wind.
Two letters and a card lay on the hall floor. He stooped and gathered them. Mrs Marion Bloom. His quickened heart slowed at once. Bold handwriting. Mrs Marion.
—Poldy!
Entering the bedroom he half-closed his eyes and walked through warm yellow twilight toward her tousled head.
—Who are the letters for?
He looked at them. Mullingar. Milly.
—A letter for me from Milly, he said carefully, and a card to you. And a letter for you.
He laid her card and letter on the twill bedspread near the curve of her knees.
—Do you want the blind up?
Letting the blind up by gentle tugs halfway, his backward eye saw her glance at the letter and tuck it under her pillow.
—That do? he asked, turning.
She was reading the card, propped on her elbow.
—She got the things, she said.
He waited till she had laid the card aside and curled herself back slowly with a snug sigh.
—Hurry up with that tea, she said. I'm parched.
—The kettle is boiling, he said.
But he paused to clear the chair: her striped petticoat, tossed dirty laundry: and lifted it all in an armful onto the foot of the bed.
As he went down the kitchen stairs she called:
—Poldy!
—What?
—Scald the teapot.

On the boil sure enough: a plume of steam from the spout. He scalded and rinsed out the teapot and put in four full spoons of tea, tilting the kettle to let the water flow in. Having set it to brew, he took off the kettle, crushed the pan flat on the live coals and watched the lump of butter slide and melt. While he unwrapped the kidney the cat meowed hungrily against him. Give her too much meat and she won't catch mice. They say cats won't eat pork. Kosher. Here. He let the blood-smeared paper fall to her and dropped the kidney amid the sizzling butter sauce. Pepper. He sprinkled it through his fingers in rings from the chipped egg cup.
Then he slit open his letter, glancing down the page and across. Thanks: new hat: Mr Coghlan: Lough Owel picnic: young student: Blazes Boylan's seaside girls.

The tea was brewed. He filled his own moustache cup, a mock Crown Derby, smiling. Silly Milly's birthday gift. Only five she was then. No wait: four. I gave her the amber-colored necklace she broke. Putting pieces of folded brown paper in the letterbox for her. He smiled, pouring.

Oh, Milly Bloom, you are my darling.
You are my looking glass from night to morning.
I'd rather have you without a farthing
Than Katey Keogh with her donkey and garden.

Poor old Professor Goodwin. Dreadful old case. Still, he was a courteous old fellow. Old-fashioned way he used to escort Molly off the stage. And the little mirror in his top hat. The night Milly brought it into the parlor. Oh, look what I found in Professor Goodwin's hat! We all laughed. Sex awakening even then. Cheeky little thing she was.

He prodded a fork into the kidney and flipped it over: then fitted the teapot on the tray. Its bump bumped as he took it up. Everything on it? Bread and butter, four slices, sugar, spoon, her cream. Yes. He carried it upstairs, his thumb hooked in the teapot handle.
Nudging the door open with his knee he carried the tray in and set it on the chair by the bedhead.
—What a time you were! she said.

She set the brass bedstead jingling as she raised herself briskly, an elbow on the pillow. He looked calmly down at her body and between her large soft breasts, sloping within her nightdress like a goat's udder. The warmth of her lying body rose in the air, mingling with the fragrance of the tea she poured.
A strip of torn envelope peeked from under the dimpled pillow. In the act of leaving he stopped to straighten the bedspread.
—Who was the letter from? he asked.
Bold handwriting. Marion.
—Oh, Boylan, she said. He's bringing the program.
—What are you singing?
—Là ci darem — the duet from Don Giovanni — with J. C. Doyle, she said, and Love's Old Sweet Song.
Her full lips, drinking, smiled. Rather stale smell that incense leaves the next day. Like foul flower water.
—Would you like the window open a little?
She doubled a slice of bread into her mouth, asking:
—What time is the funeral?
—Eleven, I think, he answered. I didn't see the paper.
Following the pointing of her finger he picked up a leg of her soiled drawers from the bed. No? Then, a twisted grey garter looped round a stocking: rumpled, shiny sole.
—No: that book.
Other stocking. Her petticoat.
—It must have fallen down, she said.

He felt here and there. I would and I wouldn't — the aria from Don Giovanni. Wonder if she pronounces that right: voglio. Not in the bed. Must have slid down. He stooped and lifted the bed valance. The book, fallen, sprawled against the bulge of the orange-keyed chamber pot.
—Show here, she said. I put a mark in it. There's a word I wanted to ask you.

She swallowed a gulp of tea from her cup, held by the body since the handle was broken, and, having wiped her fingertips smartly on the blanket, began to search the text with the hairpin till she reached the word.
—Met him what? he asked.
—Here, she said. What does that mean?
He leaned down and read near her polished thumbnail.
—Metempsychosis?
—Yes. Who's he when he's at home?
—Metempsychosis, he said, frowning. It's Greek: from the Greek. It means the transmigration of souls.
—Oh, come off it! she said. Tell us in plain words.

He smiled, glancing sideways at her mocking eyes. The same young eyes. The first night after the party games. Dolphin's Barn. He turned over the smudged pages. Ruby: the Pride of the Ring. Hello. Illustration. Fierce Italian with carriage whip. Must be Ruby, pride of the ring, on the floor naked. Sheet kindly provided. The monster Maffei relented and flung his victim from him with an oath. Cruelty behind it all. Drugged animals. Trapeze at Hengler's circus. Had to look the other way. Mob gaping. Break your neck and we'll split our sides laughing. Whole families of them. Bend their bones young so they — metempsychosis. That we live after death. Our souls. That a man's soul after he dies. Dignam's soul...
—Did you finish it? he asked.
—Yes, she said. There's nothing dirty in it. Is she in love with the first fellow the whole time?
—Never read it. Do you want another?
—Yes. Get another of Paul de Kock's. Nice name he has.
She poured more tea into her cup, watching it flow sideways.
Must get that library book from Capel Street renewed or they'll write to Kearney, my guarantor. Reincarnation: that's the word.

—Some people believe, he said, that we go on living in another body after death, that we lived before. They call it reincarnation. That we all lived before on the earth thousands of years ago or on some other planet. They say we have forgotten it. Some say they remember their past lives.
The sluggish cream wound curdling spirals through her tea. Better remind her of the word: metempsychosis. An example would be better. An example?

The painting of The Bath of the Nymph over the bed. Given away free with the Easter issue of Photo Bits magazine: Splendid masterpiece in art colors. Tea before you put milk in. Not unlike her with her hair down: slimmer. Three shillings and six I gave for the frame. She said it would look nice over the bed. Naked nymphs: Greece: and for instance all the people who lived then.
He turned the pages back.
—Metempsychosis, he said, is what the ancient Greeks called it. They used to believe you could be changed into an animal or a tree, for instance. What they called nymphs, for example.
Her spoon stopped stirring the sugar. She gazed straight before her, breathing in through her arched nostrils.
—There's a smell of burning, she said. Did you leave anything on the fire?
—The kidney! he cried suddenly.

He crammed the book roughly into his inner pocket and, stubbing his toes against the broken dresser, hurried out toward the smell, stepping hastily down the stairs with the flurried legs of a stork. Sharp smoke shot up in an angry jet from a side of the pan. By prodding a fork prong under the kidney he detached it and flipped it turtle on its back. Only a little burnt. He tossed it off the pan onto a plate and let the scanty brown gravy trickle over it.

Cup of tea now. He sat down, cut and buttered a slice of bread. He sheared away the burnt flesh and flung it to the cat. Then he put a forkful into his mouth, chewing with appreciation the savory tender meat. Done to a turn. A mouthful of tea. Then he cut dice of bread, sopped one in the gravy and put it in his mouth. What was that about some young student and a picnic? He smoothed out the letter at his side, reading it slowly as he chewed, sopping another die of bread in the gravy and raising it to his mouth.
Dearest Daddy

Thanks ever so much for the lovely birthday present. It suits me splendidly. Everyone says I'm quite the belle in my new hat. I got mummy's lovely box of creams and am writing to thank her. They are lovely. I am getting on swimmingly in the photography business now. Mr Coghlan took one of me and Mrs. Will send it when it's developed. We did great business yesterday. Fair day and all the country people were in. We are going to Lough Owel on Monday with a few friends for a picnic. Give my love to mummy and to yourself a big kiss and thanks. I hear them at the piano downstairs. There is going to be a concert in the Greville Arms on Saturday. There is a young student who comes here some evenings named Bannon, his cousins or something are very well-to-do, and he sings Boylan's (I was on the point of writing Blazes Boylan's) song about those seaside girls. Tell him silly Milly sends my best regards. I must now close with fondest love

Your fond daughter
Milly
P.S. Excuse bad writing, am in a hurry. Byebye.
M.

Fifteen yesterday. Curious, the fifteenth of the month too. Her first birthday away from home. Separation. Remember the summer morning she was born, running to fetch Mrs Thornton in Denzille Street. Jolly old woman. Lots of babies she must have helped into the world. She knew from the first that poor little Rudy wouldn't live. Well, God is good, sir. She knew at once. He would be eleven now if he had lived.

His vacant face stared pityingly at the postscript. Excuse bad writing. Hurry. Piano downstairs. Coming out of her shell. That row with her in the XL Café about the bracelet. Wouldn't eat her cakes or speak or look. Little madam. He sopped more dice of bread in the gravy and ate piece after piece of kidney. Twelve and six a week. Not much. Still, she might do worse. Music hall stage. Young student. He drank a gulp of cooler tea to wash down his meal. Then he read the letter again: twice.

Oh, well: she knows how to look after herself. But what if not? No, nothing has happened. Of course it might. Wait in any case till it does. A wild one. Her slim legs running up the staircase. Destiny. Ripening now. Vain: very.

He smiled with troubled affection at the kitchen window. The day I caught her in the street pinching her cheeks to make them red. A little anemic. Was breastfed too long. On the Erin's King excursion boat that day around the Kish lighthouse. Damned old tub pitching about. Not a bit scared. Her pale blue scarf loose in the wind with her hair.

All dimpled cheeks and curls,
Your head it simply swirls.
Seaside girls. Torn envelope. Hands stuck in his trouser pockets, the coachman off for the day, singing. Friend of the family. Swirls, he says. Pier with lamps, summer evening, band.

Those girls, those girls,
Those lovely seaside girls.
Milly too. Young kisses: the first. Far away now, past. Mrs Marion. Reading, lying back now, counting the strands of her hair, smiling, braiding.

A soft pang, regret, flowed down his backbone, increasing. It will happen, yes. Can't prevent it. Useless: can't stop it. Girl's sweet light lips. Will happen too. He felt the flowing pang spread over him. Useless to move now. Lips kissed, kissing, kissed. Full sticky woman's lips.

Better where she is, down there in Mullingar: away. Keep her busy. She wanted a dog to pass the time. Might take a trip down there. August bank holiday, only two and six for a return ticket. Six weeks off, however. Might wangle a press pass. Or through M'Coy.

The cat, having cleaned all her fur, returned to the meat-stained paper, nosed at it and stalked to the door. She looked back at him, meowing. Wants to go out. Wait before a door — sometime it will open. Let her wait. Has the fidgets. Electric. Thunder in the air. Was washing behind her ear with her back to the fire too.
He felt heavy, full: then a gentle loosening of his bowels. He stood up, undoing the waistband of his trousers. The cat meowed to him.
—Meow! he said in answer. Wait till I'm ready.
Heaviness: hot day coming. Too much trouble to go upstairs to the landing.
A paper. He liked to read on the toilet. Hope no one comes knocking just as I'm.

In the table drawer he found an old issue of Titbits magazine. He folded it under his armpit, went to the door and opened it. The cat went up in soft bounds. Ah, wanted to go upstairs, curl up in a ball on the bed.
Listening, he heard her voice:
—Come, come, pussy. Come.
He went out through the back door into the garden: stood to listen toward the next garden. No sound. Perhaps hanging clothes out to dry. The maid was in the garden. Fine morning.

He bent down to look at a lean file of spearmint growing by the wall. Make a summerhouse here. Scarlet runner beans. Virginia creepers. Need to manure the whole place, scabby soil. A coat of sulfur treatment. All soil's like that without fertilizer. Household scraps. Loam — what is this stuff? The hens in the next garden: their droppings are very good top dressing. Best of all though are cattle, especially when they're fed on those oil cakes. Mulch of dung. Best thing to clean ladies' kid gloves, too. Dirty cleans. Ashes too. Reclaim the whole place. Grow peas in that corner there. Lettuce. Always have fresh greens then. Still, gardens have their drawbacks. That bee or bluebottle here last Whit Monday.

He walked on. Where is my hat, by the way? Must have put it back on the peg. Or lying on the floor. Funny I don't remember that. Hall stand too full. Four umbrellas, her raincoat. Picking up the letters. Drago's barber shop bell ringing. Queer I was just thinking about that. Brown brilliantined hair over his collar. Just had a wash and trim. Wonder if I have time for a bath this morning. Tara Street baths. The clerk in the ticket booth there helped James Stephens escape, they say. O'Brien.
Deep voice that butcher Dlugacz has. Agendath what is it? Now, my miss. Enthusiast.

He kicked open the rickety door of the outhouse. Better be careful not to get these trousers dirty for the funeral. He went in, ducking his head under the low lintel. Leaving the door ajar, amid the stench of moldy whitewash and stale cobwebs he undid his suspenders. Before sitting down he peered through a chink up at the next-door windows. The king was in his counting house. Nobody.

Squatting on the seat he unfolded his paper, turning its pages over on his bared knees. Something new and easy. No great hurry. Save it for a bit. Our prize feature: Matcham's Masterstroke. Written by Mr Philip Beaufoy, Playgoers' Club, London. Payment at the rate of one guinea a column has been made to the writer. Three and a half columns. Three pounds three. Three pounds, thirteen and six.

Quietly he read, holding himself back, the first column and, yielding but resisting, began the second. Midway, his last resistance giving way, he allowed his bowels to ease themselves quietly as he read, reading still patiently, that slight constipation of yesterday quite gone. Hope it's not too big — don't want piles again. No, just right. So. Ah! Binding. One tablet of cascara laxative. Life might be like this story. It didn't move or touch him but it was something quick and neat. They'll print anything now. Silly season. He read on, seated calm above his own rising smell. Neat, certainly. Matcham often thinks of the masterstroke by which he won the laughing witch who now. Begins and ends with a moral. Hand in hand. Smart. He glanced back through what he had read and, while feeling his urine flow quietly, he kindly envied Mr Beaufoy who had written it and received payment of three pounds, thirteen and six.

Might try writing a sketch myself. By Mr and Mrs L. M. Bloom. Invent a story around some proverb. Which one? I used to try jotting down on my shirt cuff what she said while dressing. Don't like dressing together. Nicked myself shaving. Biting her lower lip, hooking the fastener of her skirt. Timing her. 9:15. Did Roberts pay you yet? 9:20. What was Gretta Conroy wearing? 9:23. What possessed me to buy this comb? 9:24. I'm bloated after that cabbage. A speck of dust on the patent leather of her boot.

Rubbing smartly in turn each sole against her stockinged calf. Morning after the charity ball when May's band played Ponchielli's Dance of the Hours. Explain that: morning hours, noon, then evening coming on, then night hours. Brushing her teeth. That was the first night. Her head dancing. Her fan clicking. Is that Boylan well off? He has money. Why? I noticed he smelled good when we were dancing. No use hinting. Allude to it. Strange kind of music that last night. The mirror was in shadow. She rubbed her hand mirror briskly on her woolen undershirt against her full swaying breast. Peering into it. Lines around her eyes. It just wouldn't work out somehow.
Evening hours, girls in grey gauze. Night hours then: black with daggers and eye masks. Poetic idea: pink, then golden, then grey, then black. Still, true to life also. Day: then the night.

He tore away half the prize story sharply and wiped himself with it. Then he pulled up his trousers, buckled his suspenders and buttoned himself. He pulled back the jerky shaky door of the outhouse and came forth from the gloom into the air.
In the bright light, lightened and cooled in body, he examined carefully his black trousers: the cuffs, the knees, the backs of the knees. What time is the funeral? Better find out in the paper.
A creak and a dark whir in the air high up. The bells of George's church. They tolled the hour: loud dark iron.

Heigho! Heigho!
Heigho! Heigho!
Heigho! Heigho!
Quarter to. There again: the overtone following through the air. A third.
Poor Dignam!

chapters.title: Episode 5 — Lotus Eaters
paragraphs: Past lorries along Sir John Rogerson's Quay Mr Bloom walked soberly, past Windmill Lane, Leask's the linseed crusher's, the postal telegraph office. Could have given that address too. And past the sailors' home. He turned from the morning noises of the quayside and walked through Lime Street. By Brady's cottages a boy employed to collect animal skins lounged, his bucket of offal dangling, smoking a chewed cigarette butt. A smaller girl with scars of eczema on her forehead eyed him, listlessly holding her battered toy hoop. Tell him if he smokes he won't grow. Oh, let him! His life isn't such a bed of roses. Waiting outside pubs to bring Dad home. Come home to Ma, Da. Slack hour: won't be many there. He crossed Townsend Street, passed the frowning facade of Bethel chapel. El, yes: house of: Aleph, Beth — Hebrew letters. And past Nichols' the undertaker. The funeral is at eleven. Time enough. I dare say Corny Kelleher landed the job for O'Neill's funeral home. Singing with his eyes shut. Corny. Met her once in the park. In the dark. What a lark. Police informer. She told him her name and address along with my tooraloom tooraloom tay. Oh, he surely landed it. Bury him cheap in a whatyoumaycall. With my tooraloom, tooraloom, tooraloom, tooraloom.

In Westland Row he halted before the window of the Belfast and Oriental Tea Company and read the labels on the lead-papered packets: choice blend, finest quality, family tea. Rather warm. Tea. Must get some from Tom Kernan. Couldn't ask him at a funeral, though. While his eyes still read blandly he took off his hat quietly, inhaling his hair oil, and sent his right hand with slow grace over his brow and hair. Very warm morning. Under their dropped lids his eyes found the tiny bow of the leather headband inside his high grade ha — the t worn off. Just there. His right hand came down into the bowl of his hat. His fingers found quickly a card behind the headband and transferred it to his waistcoat pocket.

So warm. His right hand once more, more slowly, went over his brow and hair. Then he put on his hat again, relieved: and read again: choice blend, made of the finest Ceylon brands. The Far East. Lovely spot it must be: the garden of the world, big lazy leaves to float about on, cactuses, flowery meadows, snaky vines they call lianas. Wonder if it's really like that. Those Sri Lankans lounging around in the sun in sweet idleness, not doing a hand's turn all day. Sleeping six months out of twelve. Too hot to quarrel. Effect of the climate. Lethargy. Flowers of idleness. The air feeds most. Nitrogen. Hothouse in the Botanic Gardens. Sensitive plants. Water lilies. Petals too tired to. Sleeping sickness in the air. Walk on rose petals. Imagine trying to eat tripe and cow heel there. Where was that picture I saw somewhere? Ah yes, in the Dead Sea, a man floating on his back, reading a book with a parasol open. Couldn't sink if you tried: so thick with salt. Because the weight of the water, no, the weight of the body in the water is equal to the weight of the what? Or is it the volume is equal to the weight? It's a law, something like that. Vance in high school cracking his finger joints, teaching. The college curriculum. Cracking curriculum. What is weight really when you say the weight? Thirty-two feet per second per second. Law of falling bodies: per second per second. They all fall to the ground. The earth. It's the force of gravity of the earth that is the weight.

He turned away and sauntered across the road. How did that girl walk with her sausages? Like that, something. As he walked he took the folded Freeman's Journal from his side pocket, unfolded it, rolled it lengthwise into a baton and tapped it at each sauntering step against his trouser leg. Casual air: just dropping in to check. Per second per second. Per second for every second it means. From the curb he darted a keen glance through the door of the post office. Too late for the box. Post here. No one. In.
He handed the card through the brass grill.
—Are there any letters for me? he asked.

While the postmistress searched a pigeonhole he gazed at the recruiting poster with soldiers of all branches on parade: and held the tip of his rolled paper against his nostrils, smelling the fresh-printed ink on paper. No answer probably. Went too far last time.
The postmistress handed him back through the grill his card with a letter. He thanked her and glanced rapidly at the typed envelope.

Henry Flower Esq,
c/o P.O. Westland Row,
City.

Answered anyway. He slipped card and letter into his side pocket, reviewing again the soldiers on parade. Where's old Tweedy's regiment? Retired soldier. There: bearskin cap and hackle plume. No, he's a grenadier. Pointed cuffs. There he is: Royal Dublin Fusiliers. Redcoats. Too showy. That must be why the women go after them. Uniform. Easier to enlist and drill. Maud Gonne's letter about removing them from O'Connell Street at night: disgrace to our Irish capital. Griffith's paper is on the same tack now: an army rotten with venereal disease: overseas or half-seas-over empire. They look half-baked: hypnotized. Eyes front. Mark time. Table: able. Bed: ed. The King's Own regiment. You never see him dressed up as a fireman or a policeman. A Freemason, yes.

He strolled out of the post office and turned to the right. Talk: as if that would fix anything. His hand went into his pocket and a forefinger felt its way under the flap of the envelope, ripping it open in jerks. Women will pay a lot of attention, I don't think. His fingers drew out the letter and crumpled the envelope in his pocket. Something pinned on: photo perhaps. Hair? No.
M'Coy. Get rid of him quickly. Takes me out of my way. Hate company when you.
—Hello, Bloom. Where are you off to?
—Hello, M'Coy. Nowhere in particular.
—How's the body?
—Fine. How are you?
—Just keeping alive, M'Coy said.
His eyes on the black tie and clothes, he asked with low respect:
—Is there any... no trouble I hope? I see you're...
—Oh, no, Mr Bloom said. Poor Dignam, you know. The funeral is today.
—To be sure, poor fellow. So it is. What time?
A photo it isn't. A badge maybe.
—E...eleven, Mr Bloom answered.
—I must try to get out there, M'Coy said. Eleven, is it? I only heard last night. Who was telling me? Holohan. You know Hoppy?
—I know.

Mr Bloom gazed across the road at the carriage drawn up before the door of the Grosvenor Hotel. The porter hoisted the suitcase up on the back. She stood still, waiting, while the man — husband, brother, someone like her — searched his pockets for change. Stylish kind of coat with that roll collar, warm for a day like this, looks like blanket cloth. The careless way she stands with her hands in those patch pockets. Like that haughty woman at the polo match. Women all about social standing until you touch the right spot. Handsome is as handsome does. Reserved but about to yield. The honorable Mrs so-and-so, and Brutus is an honorable man. Have her once and take the starch out of her.
—I was with Bob Doran — he's on one of his periodic binges — and what do you call him, Bantam Lyons. Just down there in Conway's pub we were.

Doran, Lyons in Conway's. She raised a gloved hand to her hair. In came Hoppy Holohan. Having a drink. Drawing back his head and gazing from beneath his half-lowered eyelids he saw the bright fawn-colored skin shine in the glare, the braided hem of her dress. I can see clearly today. Moisture in the air gives long sight perhaps. M'Coy talking of one thing or another. Lady's hand. Which side will she get up on?
—And he said: Sad thing about our poor friend Paddy! What Paddy? I said. Poor little Paddy Dignam, he said.

Off to the country: Broadstone station probably. High brown boots with laces dangling. Well-turned foot. What is he fumbling with that change for? Sees me looking. Always watching for the other fellow's eye. Good fallback. Two strings to her bow.
—Why? I said. What's wrong with him? I said.
Proud: rich: silk stockings.
—Yes, Mr Bloom said.
He shifted a little to the side of M'Coy's talking head. She's getting up any minute.

—What's wrong with him? he said. He's dead, he said. And, honest to God, he choked up. Is it Paddy Dignam? I said. I couldn't believe it when I heard it. I was with him no later than last Friday — or was it Thursday? — in the Arch pub. Yes, he said. He's gone. He died on Monday, poor fellow.
Watch! Watch! Silk flash, rich stockings, white. Watch!
A heavy tram honking its gong swung between them.

Lost it. Damn your noisy horn. Feels locked out of paradise. The fairy tale of the outcast. Always happening like that. The very moment. That girl in the Eustace Street hallway Monday — was it? — adjusting her garter. Her friend covering the display. Team spirit. Well, what are you gaping at?
—Yes, yes, Mr Bloom said after a dull sigh. Another gone.
—One of the best, M'Coy said.
The tram passed. They drove off toward the Loop Line bridge, her rich gloved hand on the steel grip. Flicker, flicker: the lace trim of her hat in the sun: flicker, flick.
—Wife well, I suppose? M'Coy's changed voice said.
—Oh, yes, Mr Bloom said. Tiptop, thanks.
He unrolled the newspaper baton idly and read idly:

What is home without
Plumtree's Potted Meat?
Incomplete.
With it an abode of bliss.
—My wife has just got an engagement. At least it's not settled yet.
Suitcase talk again. By the way, no harm in it. I'm past that, thanks.
Mr Bloom turned his large-lidded eyes with unhurried friendliness.
—My wife too, he said. She's going to sing at a fancy affair in the Ulster Hall, Belfast, on the twenty-fifth.
—That so? M'Coy said. Glad to hear that, old man. Who's organizing it?

Mrs Marion Bloom. Not up yet. Queen was in her bedroom eating bread and. No book. Blackened playing cards laid along her thigh in rows of seven. Dark lady and fair man. Letter. Cat, furry black ball. Torn strip of envelope.

Love's
Old
Sweet
Song
Comes lo-ove's old...
—It's a kind of a tour, don't you see, Mr Bloom said thoughtfully. Sweeeeet song. There's a committee formed. Part shares and part profits.
M'Coy nodded, picking at his moustache stubble.
—Oh, well, he said. That's good news.
He moved to go.
—Well, glad to see you looking fit, he said. See you around.
—Yes, Mr Bloom said.

—Tell you what, M'Coy said. You might put down my name at the funeral, will you? I'd like to go but I mightn't be able, you see. There's a drowning case at Sandycove that may turn up and then the coroner and I would have to go down if the body is found. You just put in my name if I'm not there, will you?
—I'll do that, Mr Bloom said, moving to get away. That'll be all right.
—Right, M'Coy said brightly. Thanks, old man. I'd go if I possibly could. Well, cheerio. Just C. P. M'Coy will do.
—That will be done, Mr Bloom answered firmly.

Didn't catch me napping with that trick. The quick touch. Easy mark. I'd love my job — him borrowing my suitcase. Leather. Capped corners, riveted edges, double action lever lock. Bob Cowley lent him his for the Wicklow regatta concert last year and never heard another word about it from that day to this.

Mr Bloom, strolling toward Brunswick Street, smiled. My wife has just got an. Reedy freckled soprano voice. Sharp-featured nose. Nice enough in its way: for a little ballad. No guts in it. You and me, don't you know: in the same boat. Flattery. Would really annoy you. Can't he hear the difference? Think he swings that way a bit. Against my grain somehow. Thought that mention of Belfast would give him the hint. I hope that smallpox up there doesn't get worse. Suppose she wouldn't let herself be vaccinated again. Your wife and my wife.
Wonder is he following me?

Mr Bloom stood at the corner, his eyes wandering over the multicolored billboard posters. Cantrell and Cochrane's Ginger Ale (Aromatic). Clery's Summer Sale. No, he's going on straight. Hello. Leah playing tonight. Mrs Bandmann Palmer. Like to see her again in that. She played Hamlet last night. Male impersonator. Perhaps Hamlet was a woman. Why Ophelia committed suicide. Poor Papa! How he used to talk about Kate Bateman in that role. Outside the Adelphi Theatre in London he waited all afternoon to get in. Year before I was born that was: sixty-five. And Ristori in Vienna. What's the actual name of the play? By Mosenthal, it is. Rachel, is it? No. The scene he always talked about where the old blind Abraham recognizes the voice and puts his fingers on his face.
Nathan's voice! His son's voice! I hear the voice of Nathan who left his father to die of grief and misery in my arms, who left the house of his father and left the God of his father.
Every word is so deep, Leopold.
Poor Papa! Poor man! I'm glad I didn't go into the room to look at his face. That day! Oh, dear! Oh, dear! Pfew! Well, perhaps it was the best for him.
Mr Bloom went round the corner and passed the drooping cab horses at the stand. No use thinking of it anymore. Feeding time. Wish I hadn't met that M'Coy fellow.

He came nearer and heard a crunching of gilded oats, the gently champing teeth. Their full bulging eyes regarded him as he passed, amid the sweet oaty reek of horse urine. Their paradise. Poor old nags! They know and care damn all about anything with their long noses stuck in feed bags. Too full for words. Still, they get their feed all right and their rest. Gelded too: a stump of black rubber wagging limp between their haunches. Might be happy all the same that way. Decent-looking poor brutes. Still, their neigh can be very irritating.
He drew the letter from his pocket and folded it into the newspaper he carried. Might just walk into her here. The side lane is safer.

He passed the cabmen's shelter. Curious, the life of drifting cab drivers. All weathers, all places, fare or waiting, no will of their own. I want to and I don't. Like to give them the odd cigarette. Sociable types. Shout a few words as they pass. He hummed:

Là ci darem la mano — Give me your hand —
La la lala la la.

He turned into Cumberland Street and, going on some paces, halted in the shelter of the station wall. No one about. Meade's timber yard. Piled planks. Ruins and tenements. Stepping carefully he passed over a hopscotch court with its forgotten stone marker. Not a soul. Near the timber yard a child squatted playing marbles alone, shooting with a practiced thumb. A wise tabby cat, a blinking sphinx, watched from her warm windowsill. Pity to disturb them. The Prophet Muhammad cut a piece from his cloak rather than disturb a sleeping cat. Open the letter. And once I played marbles when I went to that old dame's school. She liked the flower mignonette. Mrs Ellis's school. And Mr? He opened the letter within the newspaper.
A flower. I think it's a. A yellow flower with flattened petals. Not angry then? What does she say?
Dear Henry

I got your last letter to me and thank you very much for it. I am sorry you did not like my last letter. Why did you enclose the stamps? I am awfully angry with you. I do wish I could punish you for that. I called you naughty boy because I do not like that other word. Please tell me what is the real meaning of that word? Are you not happy in your home you poor little naughty boy? I do wish I could do something for you. Please tell me what you think of poor me. I often think of the beautiful name you have. Dear Henry, when will we meet? I think of you so often you have no idea. I have never felt myself so much drawn to a man as you. I feel so bad about. Please write me a long letter and tell me more. Remember if you do not I will punish you. So now you know what I will do to you, you naughty boy, if you do not write. O how I long to meet you. Henry dear, do not deny my request before my patience is exhausted. Then I will tell you all. Goodbye now, naughty darling, I have such a bad headache today. and write by return to your longing
Martha
P.S. Do tell me what kind of perfume does your wife use. I want to know.

He tore the flower gravely from its pin, smelled its almost-no-smell, and placed it in his breast pocket. Language of flowers. They like it because no one can hear. Or a poison bouquet to strike him down. Then walking slowly forward he read the letter again, murmuring here and there a word. Angry tulips with you darling man-flower punish your cactus if you don't please poor forget-me-not how I long violets to dear roses when we soon anemone meet all naughty nightstalk wife Martha's perfume. Having read it all he took it from the newspaper and put it back in his side pocket.

Weak joy opened his lips. Changed since the first letter. Wonder if she wrote it herself. Playing the indignant lady: a girl of good family like me, respectable character. Could meet one Sunday after mass. Thank you: not interested. Usual love games. Then running round corners. Bad as a fight with Molly. Cigar has a cooling effect. Narcotic. Go further next time. Naughty boy: punish: afraid of words, of course. Rough, why not? Try it anyway. A bit at a time.

Fingering still the letter in his pocket he drew the pin out of it. Common pin, eh? He threw it on the road. Out of her clothes somewhere: pinned together. Strange the number of pins they always have. No roses without thorns.
Flat Dublin voices bawled in his head. Those two rough girls that night in the Coombe, linked arm in arm in the rain.

Oh, Mary lost the pin of her drawers.
She didn't know what to do
To keep it up,
To keep it up.
It? Them. Such a bad headache. Having her period probably. Or sitting all day typing. Eye strain bad for stomach nerves. What perfume does your wife use. Now, could you figure out a thing like that?
To keep it up.
Martha, Mary. I saw that painting somewhere, I forget now — old master or a fake done for money. He is sitting in their house, talking. Mysterious. The two rough girls in the Coombe would listen too.
To keep it up.

Nice kind of evening feeling. No more wandering about. Just lie back there: quiet dusk: let everything go. Forget. Tell about places you've been, strange customs. The other sister, jar on her head, was getting the supper: fruit, olives, lovely cool water out of a well, stone-cold like the water fountain at Ashtown racecourse. Must carry a paper cup next time I go to the races. She listens with big dark soft eyes. Tell her: more and more: all. Then a sigh: silence. Long long long rest.
Going under the railway arch he took out the envelope, tore it swiftly to shreds and scattered them toward the road. The shreds fluttered away, sank in the damp air: a white flutter, then all sank.

Henry Flower. You could tear up a check for a hundred pounds in the same way. Simple bit of paper. Lord Iveagh once cashed a seven-figure check for a million in the Bank of Ireland. Shows you the money to be made from stout. Still, the other brother Lord Ardilaun has to change his shirt four times a day, they say. His skin breeds lice or something. A million pounds, wait a moment. Twopence a pint, fourpence a quart, eightpence a gallon of porter — no, one and fourpence a gallon of porter. One and four into twenty: about fifteen. Yes, exactly. Fifteen million barrels of porter.
What am I saying, barrels? Gallons. About a million barrels all the same.

An incoming train clanked heavily above his head, coach after coach. Barrels bumped in his head: dull porter sloshed and churned inside. The bung holes sprang open and a huge dull flood leaked out, flowing together, winding through mudflats all over the level land, a lazy pooling swirl of liquor bearing along wide-leafed flowers of its froth.

He had reached the open back door of All Hallows Church. Stepping into the porch he took off his hat, took the card from his pocket and tucked it again behind the leather headband. Damn it. I might have tried to get M'Coy to wangle a train pass to Mullingar.

Same notice on the door. Sermon by the Very Reverend John Conmee S.J. on Saint Peter Claver S.J. and the African Mission. Prayers for the conversion of Gladstone they had too when he was almost unconscious. The Protestants are the same. Convert Dr William J. Walsh D.D. to the true religion. Save China's millions. Wonder how they explain Christianity to the Chinese. They'd prefer an ounce of opium. Celestials, they call them. Rank heresy to them. Buddha, their god, lying on his side in the museum. Taking it easy with hand under his cheek. Joss sticks burning. Not like the crucifix. Crown of thorns and cross. Clever idea, Saint Patrick using the shamrock. Chopsticks? Father Conmee: Martin Cunningham knows him: distinguished-looking. Sorry I didn't ask him about getting Molly into the choir instead of that Father Farley who looked a fool but wasn't. They're trained that way. He's not going out in blue-tinted glasses with the sweat rolling off him to baptize Africans, is he? The glasses would fascinate them, flashing. Like to see them sitting around in a circle with thick lips, entranced, listening. Still life. Lap it up like milk, I suppose.
The cold smell of sacred stone called him. He trod the worn steps, pushed the swing door and entered softly by the rear.

Something going on: some religious society meeting. Pity so empty. Nice discreet place to sit next to some girl. Who is my neighbor? Jammed by the hour to slow music. That woman at midnight mass. Seventh heaven. Women knelt in the benches with crimson scarves round their necks, heads bowed. A batch knelt at the altar rails. The priest went along past them, murmuring, holding the communion wafer in his hands. He stopped at each, took out a wafer, shook a drop or two — are they in water? — off it and placed it neatly in her mouth. Her hat and head sank. Then the next one. Her hat sank at once. Then the next one: a small old woman. The priest bent down to put it into her mouth, murmuring all the time. Latin. The next one. Shut your eyes and open your mouth. What? Corpus: body. Corpse. Good idea, the Latin. Numbs them first. Hospice for the dying. They don't seem to chew it: just swallow it down. Strange idea: eating bits of a body. That's why cannibals are attracted to the concept.

He stood aside watching their blind faces pass down the aisle, one by one, and find their places. He approached a bench and seated himself in its corner, holding his hat and newspaper. These hats we have to wear. We ought to have hats molded to our heads. They settled around him here and there, heads still bowed in their crimson scarves, waiting for it to dissolve in their stomachs. Something like matzo: it's that sort of bread: unleavened shewbread. Look at them. Now I bet it makes them feel happy. Like a sweet. It does. Yes, bread of angels it's called. There's a big idea behind it, a kind of 'the kingdom of God is within you' feeling. First communicants. Penny candy. Then everyone feels like one big family party, same as in the theater, all sharing the experience. They do. I'm sure of that. Not so lonely. In our fellowship. Then coming out a bit giddy. Letting off steam. The thing is whether you really believe in it. Lourdes cures, waters of oblivion, and the Knock apparition, statues bleeding. Old fellow asleep near that confessional. Hence those snores. Blind faith. Safe in the arms of the Lord. Dulls all pain. Wake this time next year.

He saw the priest put away the communion chalice, well in, and kneel an instant before it, showing a large grey boot sole from under the lace vestment he wore. Suppose he lost the fastening of his. He wouldn't know what to do. Bald spot behind. Letters on his back: I.N.R.I.? No: I.H.S. Molly told me once when I asked. I have sinned: or no: I have suffered, it is. And the other one? Iron nails ran in.

Meet one Sunday after mass. Do not deny my request. Turn up with a veil and black bag. Dusk and the light behind her. She might be here with a ribbon round her neck doing the devotions just the same, on the sly. Their character. That fellow who turned informer against the Invincibles — the political assassins — he used to receive communion every morning. Carey was his name. This very church. Peter Carey, yes. No, Peter Claver I'm thinking of. Denis Carey. And just imagine that. Wife and six children at home. And plotting that murder the whole time. Those church crawlers, now that's a good name for them, there's always something shifty-looking about them. They're not straight businessmen either. Oh, no — she's not here: the flower: no, no. By the way, did I tear up that envelope? Yes: under the bridge.

The priest was rinsing out the chalice: then he tossed off the dregs smartly. Wine. Makes it more aristocratic than if he drank what they're used to — Guinness's stout or some temperance drink, Wheatley's Dublin Hop Bitters or Cantrell and Cochrane's Ginger Ale (Aromatic). Doesn't give them any of it: only the show wine: just the wafer for the people. Cold comfort. Pious fraud but quite right: otherwise you'd have one old boozer worse than another coming along, begging for a drink. Strange, the whole atmosphere of the. Quite right. Perfectly right, that is.

Mr Bloom looked back toward the choir loft. Not going to be any music. Pity. Who plays the organ here, I wonder? Old Glynn, he knew how to make that instrument sing, the vibrato: fifty pounds a year they say he had at Gardiner Street church. Molly was in fine voice that day, the Stabat Mater of Rossini. Father Bernard Vaughan's sermon first. Christ or Pilate? Christ, but don't keep us all night over it. Music they wanted. Everyone stood still. Could hear a pin drop. I told her to aim her voice at that corner. I could feel the thrill in the air, the fullness, the people looking up:
Who is this man.
